cards.title: What does it mean to **attach an $n$-cell** to a space $A$ along a map $\varphi : S^{n-1} \to A$?
cards.body:
Form the quotient $A \sqcup_\varphi D^n = (A \sqcup D^n)/(x \sim \varphi(x) \text{ for } x \in \partial D^n)$, where $\partial D^n = S^{n-1}$.

The map $\varphi$ is the **attaching map**, and the interior of $D^n$ becomes the new open $n$-cell. Several cells can be attached at once, each with its own map $\varphi_\alpha$.

Example: attaching a 1-cell to a single point (so $\varphi : S^0 \to \{pt\}$) gives a circle. Attaching a 2-cell to a circle by $z \mapsto z^k$ wraps the boundary of the disk $k$ times around it.

Key idea: up to homotopy equivalence, $A \sqcup_\varphi D^n$ depends only on the homotopy class of $\varphi$.

Watch out: the cell is the open disk; its closure in the new space need not be a closed disk, because the boundary can be glued down non-injectively.
cards.searchQuery: attaching an n-cell attaching map quotient disk
refs: Bredon, Topology and Geometry ch. IV

cards.title: Define a **CW complex**, including its **$n$-skeleton** and the **characteristic map** of a cell, and state the topology it carries.
cards.body:
A space $X = \bigcup_n X^n$ where $X^0$ is a discrete set and each $n$-skeleton $X^n$ arises from $X^{n-1}$ by attaching $n$-cells; $A \subseteq X$ is closed iff $A \cap X^n$ is closed in $X^n$ for all $n$.

Each cell $e^n_\alpha$ comes with a **characteristic map** $\Phi_\alpha : D^n \to X$: it maps $\operatorname{int} D^n$ homeomorphically onto the open cell and restricts on $\partial D^n$ to the attaching map $\varphi_\alpha$ (followed by inclusion). A **subcomplex** is a closed union of cells.

Example: $S^n = e^0 \cup e^n$. Take $X^0$ a point and attach $D^n$ along the constant map; the result is $D^n/\partial D^n \cong S^n$.

Watch out: $X^n$ consists of all cells of dimension at most $n$, not just the $n$-cells. The weak topology only matters when there are infinitely many cells; a finite CW complex is compact Hausdorff with its usual topology.

cards.title: Give the CW structures on $\mathbb{RP}^n$ and $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with the fewest cells, and say how the top cell is attached.
cards.body:
$\mathbb{RP}^n$ has one cell in each dimension $0,1,\dots,n$; $\mathbb{CP}^n$ has one cell in each even dimension $0,2,\dots,2n$. The top cell is attached by the quotient map from the sphere.

Precisely, $\mathbb{RP}^n = \mathbb{RP}^{n-1} \cup_p D^n$ with $p : S^{n-1} \to \mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$ the 2-to-1 quotient, and $\mathbb{CP}^n = \mathbb{CP}^{n-1} \cup_p D^{2n}$ with $p : S^{2n-1} \to \mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$ the quotient by the circle action.

Why: a point $[z_0 : \dots : z_n] \in \mathbb{CP}^n$ with $z_n \neq 0$ has exactly one representative that is a unit vector with $z_n > 0$ real. That representative is determined by $w = (z_0,\dots,z_{n-1})$ with $|w| < 1$, since $z_n = \sqrt{1 - |w|^2}$, so these points form an open disk of real dimension $2n$. As $|w| \to 1$ the point tends to $[w : 0]$, so the boundary sphere is glued on by the quotient $S^{2n-1} \to \mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$. Points with $z_n = 0$ form $\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$. The real case is identical, with the scalars $\pm 1$ in place of the unit circle.

Example: $\mathbb{RP}^1 = e^0 \cup e^1 \cong S^1$ and $\mathbb{CP}^1 = e^0 \cup e^2 \cong S^2$.

cards.title: Describe the CW structure of the closed orientable surface $\Sigma_g$ of genus $g \ge 1$ with the fewest cells, and the attaching word of its 2-cell.
cards.body:
One 0-cell, $2g$ 1-cells $a_1,b_1,\dots,a_g,b_g$, and one 2-cell attached along $a_1b_1a_1^{-1}b_1^{-1}\cdots a_gb_ga_g^{-1}b_g^{-1}$.

The 1-skeleton is a wedge of $2g$ circles, and the 2-cell is a $4g$-gon whose sides are glued in this pattern. For $g=1$ this is the torus: a square with word $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$.

Example: the Klein bottle also has one 0-cell, two 1-cells $a,b$ and one 2-cell, but the word is $aba^{-1}b$. Only the word, not the cell counts, distinguishes it from the torus.

Tip: the word gives $\pi_1(\Sigma_g) = \langle a_i, b_i \mid \prod [a_i,b_i] \rangle$ by the Seifert-van Kampen theorem.
cards.searchQuery: minimal CW structure genus g surface attaching word 2-cell Klein bottle

cards.title: Define a **cellular map** $f : X \to Y$ between CW complexes.
cards.body:
A continuous map with $f(X^n) \subseteq Y^n$ for every $n$, that is, $f$ carries the $n$-skeleton into the $n$-skeleton.

Cellular maps are the maps that respect the filtration by skeleta. They will induce maps on the cellular chain complexes. Inclusions of subcomplexes, constant maps at a 0-cell and composites of cellular maps are cellular.

Example: give $S^2$ the structure $e^0 \cup e^2$ and $S^1$ the structure $e^0 \cup e^1$. A map $S^1 \to S^2$ is cellular iff its image lies in $(S^2)^1 = \{pt\}$, so it must be constant.

Watch out: most maps are not cellular, for instance a non-constant loop in $S^2$. The cellular approximation theorem says each is nevertheless homotopic to one that is.
cards.searchQuery: cellular map CW complexes skeleton definition

cards.title: For a cellular map $f : X \to Y$ of CW complexes, the **mapping cylinder** is $M_f = \big((X \times [0,1]) \sqcup Y\big)/\big((x,1) \sim f(x)\big)$. Which cells does $M_f$ have, and what does it deformation retract onto?
cards.body:
$M_f$ has the cells of $Y$ together with, for each $k$-cell $e$ of $X$, a $k$-cell $e \times \{0\}$ and a $(k+1)$-cell $e \times (0,1)$; it deformation retracts onto $Y$.

The cell $e \times (0,1)$ is attached along $\partial e \times [0,1] \cup e \times \{0\} \cup e \times \{1\}$. The last piece lands in $f(e) \subseteq Y^k$ because $f$ is cellular, so every attaching map lands in the lower skeleton.

Other constructions: the **suspension** $SX$ collapses $X \times \{0\}$ and $X \times \{1\}$ to two separate points. It has the two new 0-cells plus a $(k+1)$-cell $e \times (0,1)$ for each $k$-cell $e$ of $X$, so $S(S^{n-1}) = S^n$.

A wedge $X \vee Y$ at 0-cells has all cells of both, minus one 0-cell. A product $X \times Y$ has cells $e_\alpha \times e_\beta$ of dimension $\dim e_\alpha + \dim e_\beta$ (a CW complex for the product topology when, for example, $X$ is finite).

Watch out: if $f$ is not cellular, $f(e)$ need not lie in $Y^k$ and this cell structure can fail; one first replaces $f$ by a homotopic cellular map, which the cellular approximation theorem (later in this unit) provides.
cards.searchQuery: mapping cylinder suspension CW structure cells product wedge

cards.title: Define the **homotopy extension property** (HEP) for a pair $(X, A)$ with $A \subseteq X$.
cards.body:
For every space $Z$, every map $X \times \{0\} \cup A \times [0,1] \to Z$ extends to a map $X \times [0,1] \to Z$.

In words (for closed $A$): if a homotopy $f_t : A \to Z$ starts at the restriction of a map $F_0 : X \to Z$, then it extends to a homotopy $F_t : X \to Z$ that starts at that same $F_0$.

The HEP is equivalent to $X \times \{0\} \cup A \times [0,1]$ being a retract of $X \times [0,1]$. Take $Z$ to be that subspace and extend its identity map to get the retraction; conversely, compose any map on the subspace with a retraction.

Key idea: every CW pair $(X,A)$ with $A$ a subcomplex has the HEP, because $X \times \{0\} \cup A \times [0,1]$ is even a deformation retract of $X \times [0,1]$ (Hatcher, Prop. 0.16).

Watch out: the HEP is not automatic. For $X = [0,1]$ and $A = \{0\} \cup \{1/k : k \ge 1\}$ the pair fails it: a retraction would have to carry each top segment $[1/(k+1), 1/k] \times \{1\}$ down through height $0$, which breaks continuity at $(0,1)$.

cards.title: State the theorem on collapsing a contractible subcomplex: what can be said about the quotient map $q : X \to X/A$?
cards.body:
If $(X,A)$ is a CW pair and $A$ is contractible, then $q : X \to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence (more generally, this holds whenever $(X,A)$ has the HEP and $A$ is contractible).

Corollary: for a CW pair $(X, A)$ let $CA = A \times [0,1]/A \times \{1\}$ be the cone on $A$. Then $X \cup CA \simeq X/A$, where $CA$ is glued to $X$ along $A \times \{0\}$.

Why: $CA$ is a contractible subcomplex of $X \cup CA$ and $(X \cup CA)/CA = X/A$, so the theorem applies.

Example: collapsing a contractible subcomplex such as a tree in a graph does not change the homotopy type.

Watch out: contractibility of $A$ alone is not what drives the proof; the HEP is used to extend the contraction over $X$.

cards.title: Outline the proof that $q : X \to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence when $(X,A)$ has the HEP and $A$ is contractible.
cards.body:
Extend a contraction of $A$ to a homotopy $F_t : X \to X$ starting at the identity; then $F_1$ factors through $X/A$ and gives a homotopy inverse of $q$.

1. Since $A$ is contractible there is $f_t : A \to A$ with $f_0 = \mathrm{id}_A$ and $f_1$ constant.
2. By the HEP, extend $f_t$ (with $F_0 = \mathrm{id}_X$) to $F_t : X \to X$ with $F_t|_A = f_t$.
3. Because $F_t(A) \subseteq A$, each $F_t$ induces $\bar F_t : X/A \to X/A$, and $\bar F_0 = \mathrm{id}$. (Continuity of the induced homotopy holds because $q \times \mathrm{id}_{[0,1]}$ is a quotient map.)
4. $F_1(A)$ is a point, so $F_1 = g \circ q$ for a continuous $g : X/A \to X$.
5. Then $g q = F_1 \simeq F_0 = \mathrm{id}_X$, and $q g q = q F_1 = \bar F_1 q$, so $q g = \bar F_1 \simeq \mathrm{id}_{X/A}$.

Watch out: the extension must keep $A$ inside $A$ at all times; that is why we extend a contraction taking place within $A$.
cards.searchQuery: proof quotient by contractible subcomplex homotopy equivalence HEP

cards.title: Give a compact subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that is a union of countably many circles through one common point, with radii tending to $0$, yet is not a CW complex.
cards.body:
The Hawaiian earring $H = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} C_n$, where $C_n$ is the circle of radius $1/n$ centered at $(1/n, 0)$; all circles pass through the origin $O$.

Why it is not CW: a CW complex is locally contractible, so $O$ would have arbitrarily small contractible neighborhoods. Every neighborhood of $O$ contains some whole circle $C_m$. The map $r_m : H \to C_m$ collapsing all other circles to $O$ is a retraction, so the inclusion $C_m \hookrightarrow H$ is not null-homotopic. A contractible neighborhood $U \subseteq H$ containing $C_m$ would make it null-homotopic.

Watch out: the infinite wedge of circles with the weak topology is a CW complex, but it is not homeomorphic to $H$. It is not compact, and it is not first countable at the wedge point.
cards.searchQuery: Hawaiian earring not CW complex locally contractible
refs: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Appendix (topology of cell complexes)

cards.title: State the **cellular approximation theorem**.
cards.body:
Every map $f : X \to Y$ between CW complexes is homotopic to a cellular map; if $f$ is already cellular on a subcomplex $A \subseteq X$, the homotopy can be chosen stationary on $A$ (a homotopy rel $A$).

Why it matters: homotopy questions can be pushed into skeleta. For example, any map $S^k \to S^n$ with $k<n$ is homotopic to a cellular one, which lands in $(S^n)^k = \{pt\}$ for the structure $e^0 \cup e^n$, so it is null-homotopic.

Key idea: the proof moves the map off the interior of cells one dimension at a time.

Watch out: both spaces must be CW complexes, but they need not be finite.

cards.title: Let $X$ be the space obtained from $S^2$ by identifying the north pole $N$ with the south pole $S$, so $X = S^2/\{N,S\}$. Show that $X \simeq S^2 \vee S^1$.
cards.body:
Add an arc $A$ joining $N$ and $S$ outside the sphere to get $Y$; collapsing $A$ gives $X$, collapsing a meridian arc $B \subset S^2$ gives $S^2 \vee S^1$, and both quotient maps are homotopy equivalences.

1. Give $S^2$ a CW structure with $N, S$ as 0-cells and the meridian $B$ from $N$ to $S$ as a 1-cell. Then $Y = S^2 \cup A$ is a CW complex and $A$, $B$ are contractible subcomplexes.
2. By the theorem on contractible subcomplexes, $Y \to Y/A$ is a homotopy equivalence, and $Y/A = S^2/\{N \sim S\} = X$.
3. Likewise $Y \to Y/B$ is a homotopy equivalence. Collapsing $B$ turns $S^2$ into another $S^2$, and the arc $A$ becomes a loop attached at the collapsed point. So $Y/B \cong S^2 \vee S^1$.
4. Hence $X \simeq Y \simeq S^2 \vee S^1$.

Tip: sanity check with $\pi_1$: identifying two points of a simply connected nice space creates one free loop, so $\pi_1(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, as for $S^2 \vee S^1$.

cards.title: What is a **$\Delta$-complex** structure on a space $X$?
cards.body:
A family of maps $\sigma_\alpha : \Delta^{n_\alpha} \to X$ (vertices ordered), injective on open simplices, covering $X$ by disjoint open simplices, whose restrictions to faces are again maps $\sigma_\beta$, with $A$ open iff every $\sigma_\alpha^{-1}(A)$ is open.

Here $\Delta^n = [v_0,\dots,v_n]$ is the standard simplex with its vertices in a fixed order, and a face keeps the induced order.

Example: the circle has a $\Delta$-complex structure with one vertex and one edge (a loop). The torus has one vertex, three edges and two triangles.

Watch out: unlike the triangles of a triangulation of a surface, simplices here may be glued to themselves and to each other along several faces: edges may share both endpoints and may be loops. The vertex orders must agree on shared faces. Every $\Delta$-complex is a CW complex whose cells are the open simplices.

cards.title: Define the **simplicial homology** groups $H_n^\Delta(X)$ of a $\Delta$-complex $X$.
cards.body:
$H_n^\Delta(X) = \ker \partial_n / \operatorname{im} \partial_{n+1}$, where $\Delta_n(X)$ is the free abelian group on the $n$-simplices $\sigma_\alpha$ and $\partial_n \sigma_\alpha = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \sigma_\alpha|_{[v_0,\dots,\widehat{v_i},\dots,v_n]}$.

The groups $\Delta_n(X)$ with the maps $\partial_n$ form a **chain complex**: $\partial_{n}\partial_{n+1} = 0$. Elements of $\ker\partial_n$ are **cycles**, elements of $\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$ are **boundaries**, and $H_n$ measures cycles that are not boundaries.

Example: the circle with one vertex $v$ and one edge $e$ has $\partial e = v - v = 0$, so $H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

Watch out: it is not yet clear that the answer is independent of the chosen $\Delta$-complex structure; that follows once simplicial homology is compared with singular homology.
cards.searchQuery: simplicial homology definition chain complex boundary Delta complex

cards.title: Compute the simplicial homology of the torus from this $\Delta$-complex structure. Take a square with the bottom and top sides both an edge $a$ (read left to right), the left and right sides both an edge $b$ (read upward), and the diagonal $c$ from lower-left (BL) to upper-right (TR). All corners are one vertex $v$. The triangles are $L = [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{BR},\mathrm{TR}]$ and $U = [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TL},\mathrm{TR}]$.
cards.body:
$H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$, $H_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

Boundaries: $\partial L = [\mathrm{BR},\mathrm{TR}] - [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TR}] + [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{BR}] = b - c + a$, and $\partial U = [\mathrm{TL},\mathrm{TR}] - [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TR}] + [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TL}] = a - c + b$. So both equal $a + b - c$.

- $\partial_1 = 0$, since every edge is a loop at $v$. Hence $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, and $\ker \partial_1 = \mathbb{Z}^3$.
- $\ker \partial_2 = \{mU + nL : m + n = 0\} = \mathbb{Z}(U - L)$, so $H_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
- $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^3/\mathbb{Z}(a + b - c) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$, with basis the classes of $a$ and $b$.

Key idea: $U - L$ is the fundamental class, the whole surface as a cycle.
cards.searchQuery: torus simplicial homology Delta complex compute H1 Z2 H2 Z

cards.title: Compute the simplicial homology of the Klein bottle from this $\Delta$-complex structure. Take a square whose bottom and top sides are both an edge $a$ (read left to right), whose left side is an edge $b$ (read upward) and whose right side is $b$ read downward. Let $c$ be the diagonal from lower-left (BL) to upper-right (TR). All corners are one vertex. The triangles are $L = [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TR},\mathrm{BR}]$ and $U = [\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TL},\mathrm{TR}]$ (vertices in this order).
cards.body:
$H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 \cong \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2 = 0$.

Faces of $L$: $[\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TR}] = c$, $[\mathrm{TR},\mathrm{BR}] = b$ (the right side read downward), $[\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{BR}] = a$. So $\partial L = b - a + c$. For $U$: $[\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TL}] = b$, $[\mathrm{TL},\mathrm{TR}] = a$, $[\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{TR}] = c$, so $\partial U = a - c + b$.

- $\partial_1 = 0$, so the cycles in degree 1 are $\mathbb{Z}^3$ with basis $a,b,c$.
- $\partial(mU + nL) = (m-n)a + (m+n)b + (n-m)c$ vanishes only for $m = n = 0$, so $H_2 = 0$.
- $H_1 = \langle a,b,c \mid a + b - c = 0,\ -a + b + c = 0 \rangle$. Adding the relations gives $2b = 0$, and the first gives $c = a + b$. So $H_1 = \langle a, b \mid 2b = 0 \rangle$.

Watch out: the torsion $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $H_2 = 0$ are what separate the Klein bottle from the torus; both have Euler characteristic 0.
cards.searchQuery: Klein bottle simplicial homology Delta complex H1 Z plus Z/2

cards.title: Let $\mathbb{RP}^2$ be a square with corners BL, BR, TR, TL and a center point $m$, where the bottom side (BL to BR) is identified with the top side read from TR to TL (call it $a$), and the right side (BR to TR) is identified with the left side read from TL to BL (call it $b$). Coning from $m$ gives a $\Delta$-complex with vertices $m$, $p = [\mathrm{BL}] = [\mathrm{TR}]$, $q = [\mathrm{BR}] = [\mathrm{TL}]$; edges $a$ ($p \to q$), $b$ ($q \to p$) and spokes $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$ from $m$ to BL, BR, TR, TL; and triangles $B = [m,\mathrm{BL},\mathrm{BR}]$, $R = [m,\mathrm{BR},\mathrm{TR}]$, $T = [m,\mathrm{TR},\mathrm{TL}]$, $L = [m,\mathrm{TL},\mathrm{BL}]$. Compute $H_*^\Delta(\mathbb{RP}^2)$.
cards.body:
$H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ (generated by the class of $a + b$), $H_2 = 0$.

Boundaries: $\partial B = a - e_2 + e_1$, $\partial R = b - e_3 + e_2$, $\partial T = a - e_4 + e_3$, $\partial L = b - e_1 + e_4$. For $\partial_1$: $a \mapsto q - p$, $b \mapsto p - q$, $e_1, e_3 \mapsto p - m$, $e_2, e_4 \mapsto q - m$.

1. $H_2 = 0$: a cycle $x_BB + x_RR + x_TT + x_LL$ has $x_B = x_L = x_R = x_T =: x$ from the coefficients of $e_1,\dots,e_4$, and the coefficient of $a$ gives $2x = 0$.
2. In $C_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2$ we have $a = e_2 - e_1 = e_4 - e_3$ and $b = e_3 - e_2 = e_1 - e_4$. Put $u = e_2 - e_4$. These relations say $e_3 - e_1 = u$ and $2u = 0$. So $C_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}e_1 \oplus \mathbb{Z}e_4 \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2\,u$.
3. $\partial_1$ is injective on $\mathbb{Z}e_1 \oplus \mathbb{Z}e_4$ (images $p - m$, $q - m$) and kills $u$. So $H_1 = \ker\partial_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\,u$, and $u = a + b$.

Why $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$: the images $q - p$, $p - m$, $q - m$ of $\partial_1$ span exactly the 0-chains whose coefficients sum to $0$.

cards.title: Define singular $n$-chains, the boundary map $\partial_n$, and the singular homology group $H_n(X)$ of a space $X$.
cards.body:
$H_n(X) = \ker\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$, where $C_n(X)$ is the free abelian group on singular simplices $\sigma : \Delta^n \to X$ (continuous maps) and $\partial\sigma = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i\, \sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,\widehat{v_i},\dots,v_n]}$.

Elements of $C_n(X)$ are **singular chains**. Why $\partial\partial = 0$: expanding $\partial\partial\sigma$ gives each face $\sigma|_{[\dots\widehat{v_j}\dots\widehat{v_i}\dots]}$ with $j<i$ twice, with signs $(-1)^{i+j}$ and $(-1)^{i+j-1}$, so everything cancels.

Key idea: no structure on $X$ is needed, and a map $f : X \to Y$ gives $f_\#\sigma = f \circ \sigma$ with $\partial f_\# = f_\#\partial$. So $f$ induces $f_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$, functorially.

Watch out: $C_n(X)$ is gigantic (free of uncountable rank already for $X = [0,1]$, although $C_n(\mathrm{pt}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$), yet $H_n$ is often tiny.
cards.searchQuery: singular homology definition singular chains boundary map

cards.title: Define the **reduced homology** $\tilde H_n(X)$ of a nonempty space $X$ and compare it with $H_n(X)$.
cards.body:
$\tilde H_n(X)$ is the homology of the augmented complex $\cdots \to C_1 \to C_0 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} \mathbb{Z} \to 0$ with $\varepsilon(\sum n_i\sigma_i) = \sum n_i$; so $\tilde H_n = H_n$ for $n > 0$ and $H_0(X) \cong \tilde H_0(X) \oplus \mathbb{Z}$.

The augmentation is a chain map because $\partial\sigma = \sigma(1) - \sigma(0)$ for a 1-simplex has coefficient sum $0$. The splitting holds because $\mathbb{Z}$ is free.

Why: it makes a point have no homology at all: $\tilde H_n(\mathrm{pt}) = 0$ for all $n$. Then $\tilde H_*(X) = 0$ for contractible $X$, and the long exact sequences later read more cleanly.

Tip: $\tilde H_0(X) = 0$ exactly when $X$ is path-connected.
cards.searchQuery: reduced homology definition augmentation H0 plus Z

cards.title: What is $H_0(X)$ in terms of the topology of $X$?
cards.body:
$H_0(X)$ is the free abelian group with one basis element for each path component of $X$.

Proof idea: every 0-chain is a cycle, so $H_0 = C_0/\operatorname{im}\partial_1$ and $\partial\sigma = \sigma(1) - \sigma(0)$. If $x,y$ lie in the same path component, a path $\sigma$ from $x$ to $y$ gives $[y] = [x]$. Conversely, the map sending a point to its path component kills every $\partial\sigma$, so it induces the inverse isomorphism.

Since each $\Delta^n$ is path-connected, the same argument shows $C_n(X)$ splits over the path components, so $H_n(X) \cong \bigoplus_\alpha H_n(X_\alpha)$.

Watch out: path components, not components. The closed topologist's sine curve is connected, but has two path components, so $H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$.
cards.searchQuery: H0 free abelian path components singular homology

cards.title: Compute $H_n(\mathrm{pt})$ for all $n \ge 0$ directly from the singular chain complex.
cards.body:
$H_0(\mathrm{pt}) = \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_n(\mathrm{pt}) = 0$ for $n > 0$.

For each $n$ there is exactly one singular simplex $\sigma_n : \Delta^n \to \mathrm{pt}$, so $C_n \cong \mathbb{Z}$. Every face of $\sigma_n$ is $\sigma_{n-1}$, hence $\partial\sigma_n = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i\sigma_{n-1}$.

This sum is $0$ for $n$ odd and $\sigma_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 2$ even. So the complex is $\cdots \xrightarrow{1} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{1} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \to 0$, with $\partial_1 = 0$, $\partial_2 = 1$, $\partial_3 = 0$, $\partial_4 = 1$, and so on.

- $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}/\operatorname{im}\partial_1 = \mathbb{Z}$.
- $n$ odd: $\ker\partial_n = \mathbb{Z} = \operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$, so $H_n = 0$.
- $n \ge 2$ even: $\partial_n$ is an isomorphism, so $\ker\partial_n = 0$ and $H_n = 0$.

Tip: with homotopy invariance this gives $\tilde H_*(X) = 0$ for every contractible $X$.
cards.searchQuery: homology of a point singular chain complex compute

cards.title: State **homotopy invariance** of singular homology.
cards.body:
If $f \simeq g : X \to Y$ then $f_* = g_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$ for all $n$; hence a homotopy equivalence induces isomorphisms on all $H_n$.

Why it matters: homology depends only on the homotopy type, so it can be computed on any convenient model. A contractible space has the homology of a point.

Example: $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\} \simeq S^{n-1}$, so $H_k(\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}) \cong H_k(S^{n-1})$ for all $k$.

Tip: to show that a map induces isomorphisms in homology, it is enough to produce a homotopy inverse.

cards.title: Outline the prism-operator proof that homotopic maps induce the same map on singular homology.
cards.body:
Build a chain homotopy $P : C_n(X) \to C_{n+1}(Y)$ from a homotopy $F : X \times [0,1] \to Y$ with $\partial P + P\partial = g_\# - f_\#$, using a subdivision of $\Delta^n \times [0,1]$ into $(n+1)$-simplices.

A **chain homotopy** between chain maps $f_\#, g_\#$ is a family $P$ with $\partial P + P\partial = g_\# - f_\#$ (here $F$ runs from $f$ to $g$).

1. Label the vertices of $\Delta^n \times \{0\}$ as $v_0,\dots,v_n$ and those of $\Delta^n \times \{1\}$ as $w_0,\dots,w_n$.
2. $\Delta^n \times [0,1]$ is the union of the $(n+1)$-simplices $[v_0,\dots,v_i,w_i,\dots,w_n]$ for $i = 0,\dots,n$.
3. Set $P(\sigma) = \sum_i (-1)^i\, F \circ (\sigma \times \mathrm{id})|_{[v_0,\dots,v_i,w_i,\dots,w_n]}$.
4. Expand $\partial P(\sigma)$. A face shared by two consecutive simplices ($v_i$ dropped from the $i$-th, or $w_{i-1}$ from the $(i-1)$-th) appears twice with opposite signs and cancels. Of the faces dropping $v_i$ or $w_i$ from the $i$-th simplex, only $[w_0,\dots,w_n]$ and $[v_0,\dots,v_n]$ survive, giving $g\sigma - f\sigma$. The faces dropping $v_j$ with $j<i$ or $w_j$ with $j>i$ lie over $\partial\Delta^n$ and add up to $-P\partial\sigma$. So $\partial P = g_\# - f_\# - P\partial$.
5. If $z$ is a cycle, $g_\# z - f_\# z = \partial P z$ is a boundary, so $f_*[z] = g_*[z]$.

Key idea: the same argument shows that any two chain-homotopic chain maps induce equal maps on homology.

cards.title: State the **Hurewicz theorem in degree 1**: what is the map $h : \pi_1(X, x_0) \to H_1(X)$ and what do we know about it?
cards.body:
For path-connected $X$, the map $h$ sending a loop $f : [0,1] \to X$ to the class of $f$ viewed as a singular 1-cycle is a surjective homomorphism with kernel the commutator subgroup, so $H_1(X) \cong \pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}$.

The map $h$ is the **Hurewicz map**. A loop is a cycle because $\partial f = f(1) - f(0) = 0$.

Example: $H_1(T^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$, $H_1(\Sigma_g) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ (the relation $\prod[a_i,b_i]$ dies in the abelianization), $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$, and $H_1$ of a wedge of $r$ circles is $\mathbb{Z}^r$.

Watch out: $H_1$ forgets non-abelian information. A path-connected space with a nontrivial perfect group as $\pi_1$ has $H_1 = 0$.

cards.title: Outline the proof that $h : \pi_1(X,x_0) \to H_1(X)$ is surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup when $X$ is path-connected.
cards.body:
Show $h$ is a well-defined homomorphism using 2-simplices, lift 1-cycles to loops using paths to $x_0$, and build a left inverse $H_1(X) \to \pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}$ to identify the kernel.

1. Well defined and multiplicative: the constant 1-simplex is $\partial$ of the constant 2-simplex; if $f \simeq g$ rel endpoints, a 2-simplex gives $f - g \in \operatorname{im}\partial$; a 2-simplex $\tau$ with edges $f$, $g$, $f\cdot g$ has $\partial\tau = g - f\cdot g + f$. Hence $h(fg) = h(f) + h(g)$.
2. Surjective: for each point $p$ pick a path $\gamma_p$ from $x_0$ to $p$ ($\gamma_{x_0}$ constant). For a cycle $z = \sum n_i\sigma_i$, replace each $\sigma_i$ by the loop $\gamma_{\sigma_i(0)}\sigma_i\bar\gamma_{\sigma_i(1)}$. The correction terms sum to zero because $\partial z = 0$, so $z$ is homologous to a sum of loops.
3. Define $\varphi : C_1(X) \to \pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}$ by $\varphi(\sigma) = [\gamma_{\sigma(0)}\sigma\bar\gamma_{\sigma(1)}]$. For a 2-simplex $\tau$, the three loops multiply to the trivial class, so $\varphi(\partial\tau) = 0$ and $\varphi$ descends to $H_1(X)$.
4. $\varphi \circ h$ is the quotient map $\pi_1 \to \pi_1^{\mathrm{ab}}$. So $h(f) = 0$ forces $[f]$ into the commutator subgroup, while commutators die in $H_1$ because it is abelian.

Watch out: the loops $\gamma_{\sigma(0)}\sigma\bar\gamma_{\sigma(1)}$ are loops for every 1-simplex, not just cycles; that is what makes $\varphi$ defined on all chains.

cards.title: Let $X = S^1 \cup_\varphi D^2$, where $\varphi : S^1 \to S^1$ is $z \mapsto z^n$ for an integer $n \ge 1$. Compute $H_1(X)$.
cards.body:
$H_1(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}/n$.

1. $X$ is path-connected, with $S^1$ as a subcomplex and a single 2-cell.
2. Attaching a 2-cell along a loop $w$ kills $w$ in the fundamental group (Seifert-van Kampen). The attaching loop is the generator $a$ of $\pi_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$ traversed $n$ times, so $\pi_1(X) = \langle a \mid a^n \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/n$.
3. This group is abelian, so by the Hurewicz theorem $H_1(X) \cong \pi_1(X)^{\mathrm{ab}} = \mathbb{Z}/n$.

Example: $n = 1$ gives a disk, so $H_1 = 0$; $n = 2$ gives $\mathbb{RP}^2$ with $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$.

Tip: more generally, if $X$ is a wedge of $k$ circles with 2-cells attached along words $w_1,\dots,w_r$, then $\pi_1(X) = \langle g_1,\dots,g_k \mid w_1,\dots,w_r \rangle$, and $H_1(X)$ is $\mathbb{Z}^k$ modulo the span of the exponent-sum vectors of the $w_j$.

cards.title: Define the **relative homology** groups $H_n(X,A)$ of a pair of spaces $A \subseteq X$.
cards.body:
$H_n(X,A)$ is the homology of the quotient chain complex $C_n(X,A) = C_n(X)/C_n(A)$, with the induced boundary map.

A **relative cycle** is a chain $z$ in $X$ with $\partial z \in C_{n-1}(A)$; it is a relative boundary if $z = \partial w + (\text{chain in } A)$.

Example: $H_1(I, \partial I) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, generated by the identity path $[0,1]$, since its boundary $[1] - [0]$ lies in $C_0(\partial I)$ and the path is not a boundary modulo $\partial I$. For $A = \varnothing$ we get back $H_n(X)$.

Watch out: this is the homology of a quotient of chain complexes, not of the quotient space $X/A$. For well-behaved pairs, such as a CW complex and a nonempty subcomplex, they are related by $H_n(X,A) \cong \tilde H_n(X/A)$ (reduced homology on the right), as shown later in this unit.

cards.title: State the **long exact sequence of a pair** $(X,A)$ in singular homology and give the connecting homomorphism explicitly.
cards.body:
$\cdots \to H_n(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_n(X) \xrightarrow{j_*} H_n(X,A) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \to \cdots$ is exact, where $\partial[z] = [\partial z]$ for a relative cycle $z$.

The class $[\partial z]$ makes sense because $\partial z \in C_{n-1}(A)$ is a cycle: $\partial\partial z = 0$. The sequence comes from the short exact sequence of chain complexes $0 \to C(A) \to C(X) \to C(X,A) \to 0$. The map $\partial$ is the **connecting homomorphism**.

The sequence ends with $H_0(A) \to H_0(X) \to H_0(X,A) \to 0$. For $A \ne \varnothing$ the same sequence holds in reduced homology.

Example: for a point $x_0 \in X$, the reduced sequence of $(X, x_0)$ gives $H_n(X, x_0) \cong \tilde H_n(X)$ for all $n$, because $\tilde H_*(x_0) = 0$.

cards.title: Outline why a short exact sequence of chain complexes $0 \to A_\bullet \xrightarrow{f} B_\bullet \xrightarrow{g} C_\bullet \to 0$ gives a long exact sequence in homology. How is the connecting map built?
cards.body:
Lift a cycle $c \in C_n$ to $b \in B_n$; then $\partial b$ lies in $A_{n-1}$ and is a cycle; define $\delta[c] = [\partial b]$.

1. $g$ is onto, so pick $b$ with $g(b) = c$.
2. $g(\partial b) = \partial c = 0$, so $\partial b = f(a)$ for a unique $a \in A_{n-1}$.
3. $f(\partial a) = \partial\partial b = 0$ and $f$ is injective, so $a$ is a cycle.
4. Independence of choices: two lifts differ by $f(a'')$ and change $a$ by $\partial a''$; changing $c$ by $\partial c''$ lets us change $b$ by $\partial b''$ without changing $\partial b$.
5. Exactness by three chases. At $H_n(C)$: if $\delta[c] = 0$ then $a = \partial a'$ and $b - f(a')$ is a cycle lifting $c$. At $H_{n-1}(A)$: if $f_*[a] = 0$ then $f(a) = \partial b$ and $\delta[g(b)] = [a]$. At $H_n(B)$: if $g(b) = \partial c'$, lift $c'$ to $b'$, so $b - \partial b' = f(a)$ with $a$ a cycle.

Watch out: $\delta$ lowers degree by one, and it is natural: a map between two short exact sequences of chain complexes gives a map between their long exact sequences, and the squares containing $\delta$ commute.

cards.title: Let $B \subseteq A \subseteq X$. Show that there is a long exact sequence $\cdots \to H_n(A,B) \to H_n(X,B) \to H_n(X,A) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A,B) \to \cdots$ and identify the connecting map $\partial$.
cards.body:
Apply the long exact sequence of a short exact sequence of chain complexes to $0 \to C(A,B) \to C(X,B) \to C(X,A) \to 0$; the connecting map is $H_n(X,A) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \to H_{n-1}(A,B)$.

1. $C(A)/C(B) \to C(X)/C(B)$ is injective because $C(B) \subseteq C(A)$, and its cokernel is $C(X)/C(A)$. So the sequence is exact.
2. The long exact sequence in homology of a short exact sequence of chain complexes gives the stated sequence.
3. For $\partial$: a relative cycle $z \in C_n(X)$ modulo $C(A)$ lifts to the class of $z$ in $C_n(X)/C_n(B)$. Its boundary $\partial z$ lies in $C_{n-1}(A)$, and the connecting map takes its class in $C_{n-1}(A)/C_{n-1}(B)$. That is the pair connecting map $[z] \mapsto [\partial z] \in H_{n-1}(A)$ followed by $H_{n-1}(A) \to H_{n-1}(A,B)$.

Tip: with $B$ a point this recovers the reduced long exact sequence of the pair $(X,A)$.

cards.title: Relate $H_k(D^n, S^{n-1})$ to the homology of a sphere ($n \ge 1$).
cards.body:
$H_k(D^n, S^{n-1}) \cong \tilde H_{k-1}(S^{n-1})$ for all $k$, the isomorphism being the connecting map $\partial$.

Why: use the long exact sequence of the pair in reduced homology. Since $D^n$ is contractible, $\tilde H_*(D^n) = 0$, so $\partial : H_k(D^n,S^{n-1}) \to \tilde H_{k-1}(S^{n-1})$ is injective (its kernel is the image of $\tilde H_k(D^n) = 0$) and surjective (its cokernel injects into $\tilde H_{k-1}(D^n) = 0$).

Example: for $n=1$, $H_1(D^1, S^0) \cong \tilde H_0(S^0) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, generated by the path from one endpoint to the other.

Key idea: together with the computation of $\tilde H_*(S^n)$ this shows $H_n(D^n,S^{n-1}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and the other groups vanish, which is the local model that the cells of a CW complex contribute.

cards.title: State the **excision theorem** for singular homology.
cards.body:
If $Z \subseteq A \subseteq X$ and the closure of $Z$ lies in the interior of $A$, then the inclusion $(X \setminus Z, A \setminus Z) \hookrightarrow (X,A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_n(X \setminus Z, A \setminus Z) \to H_n(X,A)$ for all $n$.

Equivalent form: if $A, B \subseteq X$ with $X = \operatorname{int}A \cup \operatorname{int}B$, then $(B, A \cap B) \hookrightarrow (X, A)$ induces isomorphisms on $H_n$.

Why it matters: $H_n(X,A)$ cannot see what lies deep inside $A$, so one may cut away any set whose closure sits in the interior of $A$ and work with the smaller pair.

Watch out: the hypothesis on closures is needed. For $X = [0,1]$ and $A = \{0,1\}$, excising $Z = A$ would give $H_1(X \setminus A,\varnothing) = 0$, while $H_1(X,A) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

cards.title: Outline the proof of excision via **barycentric subdivision**.
cards.body:
Subdivision gives a chain map $S : C_n(X) \to C_n(X)$, chain homotopic to the identity, that replaces each simplex by smaller ones; after enough subdivisions each simplex lies in $A$ or in $B$.

Setup: $X = \operatorname{int}A \cup \operatorname{int}B$. Let $C_n^{\mathcal U}(X) = C_n(A) + C_n(B)$ be the chains made of simplices lying in $A$ or in $B$.

1. Barycentric subdivision cuts $\Delta^n$ into simplices of diameter at most $\tfrac{n}{n+1}$ times the original diameter, so iterating makes them arbitrarily small.
2. Define the subdivision operator $S$ on singular chains, with $\partial S = S\partial$ and a chain homotopy $T$ with $\partial T + T\partial = \mathrm{id} - S$.
3. For a singular simplex $\sigma$, the sets $\sigma^{-1}(\operatorname{int}A)$, $\sigma^{-1}(\operatorname{int}B)$ cover the compact $\Delta^n$ and have a Lebesgue number, so $S^m\sigma \in C^{\mathcal U}$ for large $m$.
4. Hence the inclusion $C^{\mathcal U}(X) \hookrightarrow C(X)$ induces an isomorphism on homology, and by the five lemma so does $C^{\mathcal U}(X)/C(A) \hookrightarrow C(X)/C(A)$.
5. The chain map $C(B)/C(A \cap B) \to C^{\mathcal U}(X)/C(A)$ is an isomorphism of complexes, since $C(A) \cap C(B) = C(A \cap B)$.

Watch out: the interiors must cover $X$; covering by $A$ and $B$ alone is not enough for the Lebesgue-number step.

cards.title: For a **good pair** $(X,A)$, how is $H_n(X,A)$ related to the quotient space $X/A$?
cards.body:
$H_n(X,A) \cong \tilde H_n(X/A)$ for all $n$, induced by the quotient map, where a good pair means $A$ is nonempty, closed, and a deformation retract of some neighborhood in $X$.

Examples of good pairs: any CW pair $(X, A)$ with $A$ a nonempty subcomplex, and $(D^n, S^{n-1})$ with $D^n/S^{n-1} \cong S^n$.

Why it matters: it lets us read relative homology as the reduced homology of a quotient space, and in particular identifies $H_n(X^k, X^{k-1})$ with the reduced homology of a wedge of spheres.

It also computes wedges: if each $(X_\alpha, x_\alpha)$ is a good pair, then $\tilde H_n(\bigvee_\alpha X_\alpha) \cong \bigoplus_\alpha \tilde H_n(X_\alpha)$. Apply the theorem to $(\bigsqcup_\alpha X_\alpha, \bigsqcup_\alpha x_\alpha)$, whose relative chains split as a direct sum over $\alpha$. So a wedge of $k$-spheres has $\tilde H_k$ free abelian with one generator per sphere, and no other reduced homology.

Watch out: without the good-pair hypothesis the relative groups and the quotient can differ.

cards.title: Outline the proof that $H_n(X,A) \cong \tilde H_n(X/A)$ for a good pair.
cards.body:
Choose a neighborhood $V$ of $A$ that deformation retracts onto $A$ and compare the pairs $(X,A)$, $(X,V)$ and $(X \setminus A, V \setminus A)$ with their images in $X/A$, using the long exact sequence of a triple and excision.

1. Because $V$ deformation retracts onto $A$, $H_n(V,A) = 0$. The long exact sequence of the triple $(X,V,A)$ then shows $H_n(X,A) \to H_n(X,V)$ is an isomorphism.
2. The same holds in $X/A$: $H_n(X/A, A/A) \to H_n(X/A, V/A)$ is an isomorphism.
3. Excision removes $A$ (resp. $A/A$): $H_n(X \setminus A, V \setminus A) \to H_n(X,V)$ and $H_n(X/A \setminus A/A, V/A \setminus A/A) \to H_n(X/A, V/A)$ are isomorphisms.
4. The quotient map is a homeomorphism $(X \setminus A, V \setminus A) \to (X/A \setminus A/A, V/A \setminus A/A)$, so it induces isomorphisms; by step 3 and naturality, so does $q_* : H_n(X,V) \to H_n(X/A, V/A)$.
5. $q_*$ commutes with the isomorphisms of steps 1 and 2, so $q_* : H_n(X,A) \to H_n(X/A, A/A)$ is an isomorphism, and $H_n(X/A, A/A) = \tilde H_n(X/A)$ since $A/A$ is a point.

Watch out: the deformation retraction of $V$ onto $A$ is what makes step 1 work, and closedness of $A$ is what makes the excisions of step 3 legal (the closure of the excised set $A$ must lie in the interior of $V$).

cards.title: Compute $\tilde H_k(S^n)$ for all $k \ge 0$ and $n \ge 0$.
cards.body:
$\tilde H_k(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ if $k = n$ and $0$ otherwise.

Induct on $n$. For $S^0$ (two points), $\tilde H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and all other groups vanish. For $n \ge 1$, $(D^n, S^{n-1})$ is a good pair with $D^n/S^{n-1} \cong S^n$, so
$$\tilde H_k(S^n) \cong H_k(D^n, S^{n-1}) \cong \tilde H_{k-1}(S^{n-1}),$$
the second step from the long exact sequence with $D^n$ contractible.

Example: $H_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_2(S^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}$; $H_0(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ for $n \ge 1$ but $H_0(S^0) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ in unreduced homology.

Tip: each step shifts degree and dimension by one, which is the shape of the suspension isomorphism.

cards.title: Prove the **Brouwer fixed point theorem** with homology: every continuous map $f : D^n \to D^n$ ($n \ge 1$) has a fixed point.
cards.body:
A fixed-point-free $f$ would give a retraction $r : D^n \to S^{n-1}$, impossible because the identity of $\tilde H_{n-1}(S^{n-1}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ cannot factor through $\tilde H_{n-1}(D^n) = 0$.

1. Suppose $f(x) \ne x$ for all $x$. Define $r(x)$ as the point where the ray starting at $f(x)$ and passing through $x$ leaves the disk: $r(x) = x + t(x)(x - f(x))$, where $t(x) \ge 0$ solves $|x + t(x - f(x))| = 1$. By the quadratic formula (the discriminant is nonnegative) $t$ is continuous.
2. For $x \in S^{n-1}$ we have $t(x) = 0$, so $r|_{S^{n-1}} = \mathrm{id}$, i.e. $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}_{S^{n-1}}$.
3. Apply $\tilde H_{n-1}$: $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Z}} = r_* i_*$ factors through $\tilde H_{n-1}(D^n) = 0$, a contradiction.

Tip: this is the same argument as the fundamental-group proof for $n=2$, with $\tilde H_{n-1}$ replacing $\pi_1$ so that it works in every dimension.

cards.title: Outline the proof, using **local homology**, that $\mathbb{R}^m \not\cong \mathbb{R}^n$ for $m \ne n$. (The local homology of $X$ at $x$ is $H_k(X, X \setminus \{x\})$.)
cards.body:
The local homology $H_k(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{x\})$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ exactly for $k = n$ and is preserved by homeomorphisms, so a homeomorphism $\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ forces $m = n$.

1. Excision: if points are closed in $X$ (as in $\mathbb{R}^n$), then for an open $U \ni x$, $H_k(X, X \setminus x) \cong H_k(U, U \setminus x)$, so local homology depends only on a neighborhood of $x$.
2. For $\mathbb{R}^n$: $\mathbb{R}^n$ is contractible and $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus x \simeq S^{n-1}$, so the long exact sequence gives $H_k(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^n \setminus x) \cong \tilde H_{k-1}(S^{n-1})$, which is $\mathbb{Z}$ iff $k = n$.
3. A homeomorphism $h : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ restricts to a homeomorphism of pairs $(\mathbb{R}^m, \mathbb{R}^m \setminus x) \to (\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^n \setminus h(x))$, hence an isomorphism on all relative groups. So $m = n$.

Watch out: the proof uses only continuity of $h$ and $h^{-1}$; for diffeomorphisms the derivative gives an easy argument, but here no smoothness is assumed.

cards.title: For a subspace $A \subseteq X$, show that the inclusion induces isomorphisms $H_n(A) \to H_n(X)$ for all $n$ if and only if $H_n(X,A) = 0$ for all $n$.
cards.body:
Both directions follow from exactness of the long exact sequence of the pair.

($\Leftarrow$) If all $H_n(X,A) = 0$, then in $H_{n+1}(X,A) \to H_n(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_n(X) \to H_n(X,A)$ the outer groups vanish, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism.

($\Rightarrow$) If every $i_*$ is an isomorphism:
- $i_*$ onto gives $\ker j_* = \operatorname{im} i_* = H_n(X)$, so $j_* = 0$.
- $i_*$ injective gives $\operatorname{im}\partial = \ker i_* = 0$, so $\partial = 0$.
- Exactness at $H_n(X,A)$ says $\ker\partial = \operatorname{im} j_*$, so $H_n(X,A) = \ker\partial = \operatorname{im}j_* = 0$.

Example: if $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, then $H_n(X,A) = 0$ for all $n$.

Watch out: the condition must hold for all $n$; one vanishing relative group does not make the inclusion an isomorphism.
cards.searchQuery: inclusion induces isomorphism homology iff relative homology vanishes

cards.title: Let $A \subseteq X$ be a retract of $X$ (there is $r : X \to A$ with $r|_A = \mathrm{id}_A$). Show that $H_n(X) \cong H_n(A) \oplus H_n(X,A)$ for all $n$.
cards.body:
Since $r_*i_* = \mathrm{id}$, the long exact sequence breaks into short exact sequences $0 \to H_n(A) \to H_n(X) \to H_n(X,A) \to 0$ that split.

1. $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}_A$ gives $r_* i_* = \mathrm{id}$, so $i_*$ is injective.
2. Then $\operatorname{im}\partial = \ker i_* = 0$, so $\partial = 0$ and $j_*$ is onto (exactness at $H_n(X,A)$).
3. So $0 \to H_n(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_n(X) \xrightarrow{j_*} H_n(X,A) \to 0$ is exact, and $r_*$ is a left inverse of $i_*$.
4. A short exact sequence with a left inverse splits: $H_n(X) \cong H_n(A) \oplus \ker r_* \cong H_n(A) \oplus H_n(X,A)$.

Example: $A = S^1 \times \{pt\} \subset T^2$ is a retract via projection, so $H_1(T^2)$ contains a copy of $H_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$ as a direct summand.

Watch out: without a retraction the splitting can fail. For $S^1 \subset D^2$, $H_1(D^2) = 0$ but $H_1(S^1) \oplus H_1(D^2, S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$; indeed $S^1$ is not a retract of $D^2$, since $H_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$ would inject into $H_1(D^2) = 0$.

cards.title: State the **Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms** for a homology theory on pairs of spaces.
cards.body:
Functors $h_n(X,A)$ to abelian groups, with natural maps $\partial : h_n(X,A) \to h_{n-1}(A)$, such that: homotopy invariance, exactness of the long sequence of a pair, excision, additivity over disjoint unions, and the dimension axiom $h_n(\mathrm{pt}) = 0$ for $n \ne 0$.

Notes on each axiom:
- Homotopy invariance: homotopic maps of pairs induce the same map.
- Exactness: $\cdots \to h_n(A) \to h_n(X) \to h_n(X,A) \to h_{n-1}(A) \to \cdots$ is exact.
- Excision: $h_n(X \setminus Z, A \setminus Z) \cong h_n(X,A)$ when $\overline Z \subseteq \operatorname{int}A$.
- Additivity: $h_n$ of a disjoint union is the direct sum.
- Dimension: only $h_0(\mathrm{pt})$ can be nonzero; it is the coefficient group.

Key idea: on CW pairs, any two theories satisfying all the axioms with the same coefficient group $h_0(\mathrm{pt})$ are isomorphic. Singular homology satisfies them, by the results of this unit and the previous one; dropping the dimension axiom gives other (extraordinary) homology theories.

cards.title: How does the simplicial homology of a $\Delta$-complex compare with its singular homology?
cards.body:
For every $\Delta$-complex $X$, the natural map $H_n^\Delta(X) \to H_n(X)$ sending a simplex to the singular simplex it defines is an isomorphism for all $n$.

Why: compare the long exact sequences of the pairs $(X^k, X^{k-1})$ in the two theories. In both, the relative group is $\mathbb{Z}^{(\#k\text{-simplices})}$ in degree $k$ and $0$ otherwise (singular: a good pair with quotient a wedge of $k$-spheres). The five lemma and induction on $k$ give the isomorphism for finite-dimensional $X$; infinite-dimensional ones follow because a singular chain has compact image, which lies in a finite skeleton.

Consequence: simplicial homology is independent of the $\Delta$-complex structure, and the torus, Klein bottle and $\mathbb{RP}^2$ computations are computations of singular homology.

Tip: the same skeleton-by-skeleton induction with the five lemma drives the Eilenberg-Steenrod uniqueness theorem: theories satisfying the axioms with the same coefficient group agree on CW pairs.

cards.title: Define the **degree** of a map $f : S^n \to S^n$ for $n \ge 1$.
cards.body:
$\deg f$ is the integer $d$ such that $f_*(\alpha) = d\,\alpha$ for all $\alpha \in H_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

It is well defined because every homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is multiplication by one integer, and that integer does not depend on the choice of generator.

Properties: $\deg(\mathrm{id}) = 1$, $\deg(fg) = \deg f \cdot \deg g$, $\deg f = \deg g$ if $f \simeq g$, a constant map has degree $0$, and a homeomorphism has degree $\pm 1$.

Example: for $n=1$ the degree is the winding number, by the Hurewicz isomorphism $\pi_1(S^1) \cong H_1(S^1)$.

cards.title: Outline why the reflection $\rho : S^n \to S^n$, $\rho(x_1,\dots,x_n,x_{n+1}) = (x_1,\dots,x_n,-x_{n+1})$, has degree $-1$.
cards.body:
$\rho$ swaps the two hemispheres, and $H_n(S^n)$ sits inside $H_n(S^n, S^{n-1}) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ as the class $(1,-1)$, which $\rho_*$ sends to its negative.

Let $E = S^{n-1} = \{x_{n+1} = 0\}$ and let $D_\pm$ be the closed hemispheres.

1. In the long exact sequence of $(S^n, E)$, $H_n(E) = 0$, so $j_* : H_n(S^n) \to H_n(S^n,E)$ is injective with image $\ker\partial$.
2. $(S^n,E)$ is a good pair with quotient $S^n \vee S^n$, so $H_n(S^n,E) \cong \tilde H_n(S^n \vee S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ (reduced homology of a wedge is the direct sum), with one summand for each hemisphere.
3. Identify both $D_\pm$ with $D^n$ by vertical projection, and let $g_\pm$ be the resulting generators. Both identifications restrict to the same map on $E$, so $\partial g_+ = \partial g_-$ is a generator of $\tilde H_{n-1}(E)$. Hence $\ker\partial = \mathbb{Z}(g_+ - g_-)$.
4. $\rho$ fixes $E$ and swaps $D_\pm$ compatibly with these identifications, so $\rho_* g_\pm = g_\mp$. By naturality of $j_*$, $\rho_*$ sends $g_+ - g_-$ to $-(g_+ - g_-)$.

Tip: the generator is the "upper hemisphere minus lower hemisphere" cycle; swapping the hemispheres flips its sign.

cards.title: What is the degree of the antipodal map $a : S^n \to S^n$, $a(x) = -x$?
cards.body:
$\deg a = (-1)^{n+1}$.

Why: $a$ is the composite of the $n+1$ coordinate reflections $\rho_i$ (negate $x_i$). Each $\rho_i$ is conjugate, by a permutation $\sigma$ of the coordinates, to the reflection $\rho$ in the last coordinate, which has degree $-1$. Since $\deg(\sigma\rho\sigma^{-1}) = \deg\sigma \cdot \deg\rho \cdot \deg\sigma^{-1} = \deg\rho$, each $\rho_i$ has degree $-1$, and multiplicativity gives $(-1)^{n+1}$.

Example: for $n=1$, $a$ is rotation by $\pi$, homotopic to the identity, with degree $+1 = (-1)^2$. For $n=2$, $\deg a = -1$.

Tip: for even $n$ the antipodal map reverses orientation, so it is not homotopic to the identity.

cards.title: If $f : S^n \to S^n$ has no fixed point, what is $f$ up to homotopy, and what is $\deg f$?
cards.body:
$f$ is homotopic to the antipodal map, so $\deg f = (-1)^{n+1}$.

Why: if $f(x) \ne x$ for all $x$, the segment from $f(x)$ to $-x$ never passes through the origin. If $(1-t)f(x) - tx = 0$, then taking norms forces $t = 1/2$ and $f(x) = x$. So $\dfrac{(1-t)f(x) - tx}{\|(1-t)f(x) - tx\|}$ is a homotopy from $f$ to the antipodal map.

Consequence: any $f$ with $\deg f \ne (-1)^{n+1}$ has a fixed point.

Watch out: the converse fails. For even $n$ the reflection $\rho$ has degree $-1 = (-1)^{n+1}$ but fixes the whole equator.

cards.title: Show that every continuous $f : S^{2k} \to S^{2k}$ ($k \ge 1$) has a fixed point or a point $x$ with $f(x) = -x$.
cards.body:
Otherwise $f$ would be homotopic both to the antipodal map and to the identity, forcing $\deg f = -1$ and $\deg f = +1$.

1. Suppose $f(x) \ne x$ for all $x$. By the previous theorem $f \simeq a$ and $\deg f = (-1)^{2k+1} = -1$.
2. Suppose also $f(x) \ne -x$ for all $x$. Then $(1-t)f(x) + tx \ne 0$ (norms force $t = 1/2$ and $f(x) = -x$), so normalizing gives a homotopy $f \simeq \mathrm{id}$ and $\deg f = 1$.
3. $-1 \ne 1$, a contradiction.

Watch out: this is false for odd spheres. Rotation of $S^1$ by $\pi/2$ has no fixed point and never sends $x$ to $-x$; there is no contradiction because for odd $n$, $\deg a = (-1)^{n+1} = 1 = \deg\mathrm{id}$.

cards.title: State the **hairy ball theorem**: for which $n \ge 1$ does $S^n$ admit a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field?
cards.body:
$S^n$ has a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field if and only if $n$ is odd.

Odd $n$: view $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with $n+1$ even and set $v(x) = (-x_2, x_1, -x_4, x_3, \dots, -x_{n+1}, x_n)$, which is orthogonal to $x$ and has length $1$.

Even $n$: suppose $v$ is a nowhere-zero tangent field; rescale it to unit length. Then $F_t(x) = \cos(\pi t)\,x + \sin(\pi t)\,v(x)$ stays on $S^n$ (since $v(x) \perp x$) and is a homotopy from $\mathrm{id}$ to the antipodal map. So $1 = \deg a = (-1)^{n+1} = -1$, a contradiction.

Watch out: "tangent" means $v(x) \perp x$ for every $x$ and $v$ is continuous; a field with isolated zeros always exists.

cards.title: Which groups $G$ can act freely on $S^n$ for even $n$? (An action is **free** if no non-identity element has a fixed point; assume $G$ acts by homeomorphisms.)
cards.body:
Only the trivial group and $\mathbb{Z}/2$: if $G$ acts freely on $S^{2k}$, then $|G| \le 2$.

Why: $g \mapsto \deg g$ is a homomorphism $G \to \{\pm 1\}$ because degree is multiplicative and each homeomorphism has degree $\pm 1$. A non-identity $g$ has no fixed point, so $\deg g = (-1)^{2k+1} = -1$. Hence the kernel is trivial and $G$ embeds in $\{\pm 1\}$.

Example: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ acts freely on $S^{2k}$ by the antipodal map, with quotient $\mathbb{RP}^{2k}$.

Watch out: evenness is essential. For $S^{2k-1} \subset \mathbb{C}^k$ the group $\mu_m$ of $m$-th roots of unity acts freely by scalar multiplication, so odd spheres admit free actions of every finite cyclic group.

cards.title: Outline why the suspension $Sf : S^{n+1} \to S^{n+1}$ of $f : S^n \to S^n$, defined by $Sf[x,t] = [f(x),t]$, has the same degree as $f$.
cards.body:
The natural isomorphisms $\tilde H_{n+1}(SX) \cong H_{n+1}(CX, X) \cong \tilde H_n(X)$ commute with the maps induced by $Sf$ and $f$, so $(Sf)_*$ corresponds to $f_*$.

Write $SX = C_+X \cup C_-X$, two cones glued along $X$.

1. $C_-X$ is contractible, so the long exact sequence of $(SX, C_-X)$ gives $\tilde H_k(SX) \cong H_k(SX, C_-X)$.
2. Both pairs are good (for $X = S^n$) and $SX/C_-X = C_+X/X$, so the good-pair isomorphism gives $H_k(SX, C_-X) \cong \tilde H_k(C_+X/X) \cong H_k(C_+X, X)$.
3. The long exact sequence of $(C_+X, X)$ with $C_+X$ contractible gives $H_k(C_+X,X) \cong \tilde H_{k-1}(X)$.
4. $Sf$ maps $C_\pm X$ to $C_\pm Y$ and $X$ to $Y$, so all three isomorphisms are natural. With $X = S^n$ the isomorphism $\tilde H_{n+1}(S^{n+1}) \cong \tilde H_n(S^n)$ intertwines $(Sf)_*$ and $f_*$.

Key idea: $SX$ is two contractible cones glued along $X$, so its reduced homology is that of $X$ shifted up one degree, and the shift is natural in $X$.

cards.title: Show that $p_d : S^1 \to S^1$, $z \mapsto z^d$, has degree $d$, and explain how to get maps $S^n \to S^n$ of every degree $d \in \mathbb{Z}$.
cards.body:
$\deg p_d = d$ via the Hurewicz isomorphism, and the $(n-1)$-fold suspension of $p_d$ is a map $S^n \to S^n$ of degree $d$.

1. $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ is generated by the loop $\omega(t) = e^{2\pi i t}$, and $p_d \circ \omega$ winds $d$ times, so $(p_d)_*[\omega] = d[\omega]$.
2. The Hurewicz map $h : \pi_1(S^1) \to H_1(S^1)$ is an isomorphism ($\pi_1$ is abelian) and is natural: $(p_d)_* h = h (p_d)_*$. So $(p_d)_*$ on $H_1(S^1)$ is multiplication by $d$.
3. Suspension preserves degree, so iterating gives degree $d$ on $S^n$ for all $n \ge 1$. Negative $d$ is included: $z^{-1}$ is complex conjugation.

Tip: $d = 0$ gives a constant map, $d = 1$ the identity, $d = -1$ a reflection.

cards.title: Show that a continuous map $f : S^n \to S^n$ ($n \ge 1$) that is not surjective has degree $0$.
cards.body:
A missed point $p$ makes $f$ factor through $S^n \setminus \{p\} \cong \mathbb{R}^n$, which is contractible, so $f$ is null-homotopic and $\deg f = 0$.

1. Choose $p \notin f(S^n)$. Stereographic projection from $p$ gives $S^n \setminus \{p\} \cong \mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Write $f = i \circ f'$ with $f' : S^n \to S^n \setminus \{p\}$ and $i$ the inclusion. Then $f_* = i_* f'_*$ factors through $H_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = 0$ (as $n \ge 1$).
3. So $f_* = 0$, that is, $\deg f = 0$.

Watch out: the converse is false. The loop $e^{2\pi i t} \mapsto e^{2\pi i (1 - |2t-1|)}$ on $S^1$ goes once around and then back; it is surjective but its lift to $\mathbb{R}$ has equal endpoints, so its degree is $0$. Its suspensions give surjective degree-$0$ maps on every sphere.

cards.title: State the **local degree** formula: how is $\deg f$ computed from the preimages of one point of $S^n$?
cards.body:
If $f^{-1}(y) = \{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$ is finite, then $\deg f = \sum_i \deg f|_{x_i}$, where the local degree $\deg f|_{x_i}$ is the integer by which $f_* : H_n(U_i, U_i \setminus x_i) \to H_n(V, V \setminus y)$ acts once both groups are identified with $H_n(S^n)$.

Here $n \ge 1$, and the $U_i$ are disjoint open neighborhoods of the $x_i$ with $f(U_i) \subseteq V$ for an open neighborhood $V$ of $y$. The identifications are $H_n(U_i,U_i \setminus x_i) \cong H_n(S^n, S^n \setminus x_i) \cong H_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, by excision and then the long exact sequence of the pair ($S^n \setminus x_i$ is contractible), and likewise at $y$. Using one fixed generator of $H_n(S^n)$ on both sides is what makes the sign of the local degree well defined.

Key idea: $H_n(S^n)$ maps into $\bigoplus_i H_n(U_i,U_i\setminus x_i)$ and then, summing, into $H_n(S^n,S^n \setminus y)$.

Watch out: local degrees can be negative, so the number of preimages is not the degree. The surjective loop that runs once around $S^1$ and back has generic points with two preimages, local degrees $+1$ and $-1$, and degree $0$.

cards.title: A complex polynomial $p$ of degree $d \ge 1$ extends to a map $\hat p : \hat{\mathbb{C}} \to \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ of the Riemann sphere with $\hat p(\infty) = \infty$. Compute $\deg\hat p$, identifying $\hat{\mathbb{C}} \cong S^2$ by stereographic projection.
cards.body:
$\deg \hat p = d$.

1. $p'$ has finitely many zeros, so $p$ has finitely many critical values. Pick $y \in \mathbb{C}$ that is not one of them.
2. The equation $p(z) = y$ has exactly $d$ solutions $z_1,\dots,z_d$ (the fundamental theorem of algebra), all simple since $p'(z_i) \ne 0$. Also $\infty \notin \hat p^{-1}(y)$.
3. The local degree at each $z_i$ is $+1$. Write $p(z) = y + c(z - z_i) + R(z)$ with $c = p'(z_i) \neq 0$ and $|R(z)| \le C|z - z_i|^2$ for $|z - z_i| \le 1$. On a disk $U_i$ around $z_i$ of radius less than $\min(1, |c|/C)$, the straight-line homotopy from $p$ to $z \mapsto y + c(z - z_i)$ takes the value $y$ only at $z_i$. So does $z \mapsto y + c_t(z - z_i)$ for a path $c_t$ from $c$ to $1$ in $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. Such homotopies of maps $(U_i, U_i \setminus z_i) \to (\mathbb{C}, \mathbb{C} \setminus y)$ do not change the local degree. The end map is the translation $z \mapsto z + (y - z_i)$, which is homotopic to the identity of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$ and has $z_i$ as the only preimage of $y$, so its local degree there is its degree, $1$. (This is the topological form of the fact that holomorphic maps preserve orientation: the real Jacobian determinant is $|p'|^2 > 0$.)
4. By the local degree formula, $\deg\hat p = d \cdot (+1) = d$.

Tip: the same count shows that a rational map $P/Q$ with $P$ and $Q$ coprime has degree $\max(\deg P, \deg Q)$ on the Riemann sphere.

cards.title: Define the **cellular chain complex** of a CW complex $X$.
cards.body:
$C_n^{CW}(X) = H_n(X^n, X^{n-1})$, free abelian with one generator per $n$-cell, with $d_n = j_{n-1} \circ \partial_n$, where $\partial_n : H_n(X^n,X^{n-1}) \to H_{n-1}(X^{n-1})$ and $j_{n-1} : H_{n-1}(X^{n-1}) \to H_{n-1}(X^{n-1},X^{n-2})$.

Why free: $(X^n, X^{n-1})$ is a good pair whose quotient is a wedge of $n$-spheres, one per $n$-cell, so $H_n(X^n, X^{n-1})$ is free abelian on the $n$-cells and the other relative groups vanish.

Why $d_{n-1}d_n = 0$: it contains $\partial_{n-1} j_{n-1}$, two consecutive maps in the long exact sequence of $(X^{n-1}, X^{n-2})$.

The homology of this complex is $H_n^{CW}(X) = \ker d_n/\operatorname{im} d_{n+1}$. A generator for a cell is the image of a generator of $H_n(D^n,S^{n-1})$ under its characteristic map, so signs depend on a choice of orientation of each cell.

Example: if $X$ has cells only in even dimensions, all $d_n = 0$.

cards.title: Define the **attaching degree** $d_{\alpha\beta}$ of an $n$-cell $e^n_\alpha$ on an $(n-1)$-cell $e^{n-1}_\beta$ of a CW complex.
cards.body:
$d_{\alpha\beta}$ is the degree of the composite $S^{n-1} \xrightarrow{\varphi_\alpha} X^{n-1} \to X^{n-1}/(X^{n-1} \setminus e^{n-1}_\beta) \cong S^{n-1}$, where the second map collapses everything except the cell $e^{n-1}_\beta$ to a point.

For $n = 1$ the "degree" is interpreted on $S^0$: $d_{\alpha\beta}$ is $+1$ if the end of the 1-cell is the vertex $\beta$, minus $1$ if the start is, and the two contributions add.

Example: the 2-cell of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ is attached to the circle $\mathbb{RP}^1$ by the 2-to-1 quotient map $S^1 \to \mathbb{RP}^1$, so its attaching degree on the 1-cell is $2$. For a 2-cell attached to a wedge of circles along a word, the attaching degree on a letter is that letter's exponent sum in the word: the Klein bottle word $aba^{-1}b$ gives $0$ on $a$ and $2$ on $b$.

Watch out: the sign of $d_{\alpha\beta}$ depends on the orientations chosen for the two cells, and most of the $d_{\alpha\beta}$ are $0$.

cards.title: State the **cellular boundary formula**.
cards.body:
$d_n(e^n_\alpha) = \sum_\beta d_{\alpha\beta}\, e^{n-1}_\beta$, the sum over the $(n-1)$-cells, where $d_{\alpha\beta}$ is the attaching degree of $e^n_\alpha$ on $e^{n-1}_\beta$.

Key idea: $e^n_\alpha$ is the image of a generator $g$ of $H_n(D^n,S^{n-1})$ under the characteristic map. By naturality, $d_n(e^n_\alpha) = j_{n-1}(\varphi_\alpha)_*(\partial g)$, and $\partial g$ generates $\tilde H_{n-1}(S^{n-1})$. Projecting $H_{n-1}(X^{n-1},X^{n-2}) = \bigoplus_\beta \mathbb{Z}e_\beta$ to the $\beta$ coordinate is the collapse map of the definition, so the coefficient is its degree.

Example: for the torus, the 2-cell is attached along $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$; the coefficient on $a$ is $1 - 1 = 0$ and the same for $b$, so $d_2 = 0$.

Watch out: the sum is finite even for infinite complexes, because $\varphi_\alpha(S^{n-1})$ is compact and meets only finitely many cells.

cards.title: State the **cellular homology theorem**: how does the homology of the cellular chain complex relate to singular homology?
cards.body:
For every CW complex $X$, $H_n(X) \cong H_n^{CW}(X) = \ker d_n/\operatorname{im} d_{n+1}$ for all $n$.

Consequences: $H_n(X) = 0$ if $X$ has no $n$-cells and for $n > \dim X$; the top group $H_{\dim X}(X) = \ker d$ is free abelian; and $H_n^{CW}(X)$ does not depend on the chosen cell structure. Torsion in $H_n$ can only come from the cokernel of $d_{n+1}$.

Example: $S^n = e^0 \cup e^n$ ($n \ge 1$) has all $d_k = 0$ (for $n = 1$ because the 1-cell is a loop), so $H_k(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ for $k = 0, n$ and $0$ otherwise, in one line.

Watch out: cell counts give only upper bounds on the ranks of $H_n$; a wasteful cell structure has differentials that cancel cells.

cards.title: Outline the proof that $H_n(X) \cong \ker d_n/\operatorname{im} d_{n+1}$.
cards.body:
Show $H_n(X) \cong H_n(X^{n+1}) \cong H_n(X^n)/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$ and $H_n(X^n) \cong \ker d_n$, using the long exact sequences of the pairs $(X^k, X^{k-1})$.

1. $H_k(X^m, X^{m-1}) = 0$ for $k \ne m$ (good pair, wedge of spheres).
2. By induction with the long exact sequences, $H_k(X^n) = 0$ for $k > n$. Since $H_j(X^{m+1},X^m) = 0$ for $j \ne m+1$, the long exact sequence gives $H_n(X^m) \cong H_n(X^{m+1})$ for every $m \ge n+1$, hence $H_n(X^{n+1}) \cong H_n(X)$ (infinite complexes use compactness of singular simplices).
3. The sequence of $(X^{n+1},X^n)$ gives $H_{n+1}(X^{n+1},X^n) \xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}} H_n(X^n) \to H_n(X^{n+1}) \to 0$, so $H_n(X^{n+1}) = H_n(X^n)/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$.
4. In the sequence of $(X^n,X^{n-1})$, $H_n(X^{n-1}) = 0$, so $j_n$ is injective with image $\ker\partial_n$. Also $j_{n-1}$ is injective because $H_{n-1}(X^{n-2}) = 0$, so $\ker\partial_n = \ker d_n$.
5. Under $j_n$, $\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$ becomes $\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$, so $H_n(X) \cong \ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$.

Watch out: injectivity of $j_{n-1}$ is what lets $d_n = j_{n-1}\partial_n$ have the same kernel as $\partial_n$.

cards.title: For a finite CW complex $X$ with $c_n$ cells of dimension $n$, why does $\sum_n (-1)^n c_n = \sum_n (-1)^n \operatorname{rank} H_n(X)$? (Their common value is the **Euler characteristic** $\chi(X)$.)
cards.body:
Rank-nullity in each $C_n^{CW}$ makes the alternating sums telescope, so $\sum(-1)^n c_n = \sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X) =: \chi(X)$; in particular $\chi$ does not depend on the cell structure.

Here the rank of a finitely generated abelian group $G$ is $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}(G \otimes \mathbb{Q})$.

1. Let $Z_n = \ker d_n$ and $B_n = \operatorname{im} d_{n+1}$. From $C_n/Z_n \cong B_{n-1}$ we get $c_n = \operatorname{rank}Z_n + \operatorname{rank}B_{n-1}$.
2. By the cellular homology theorem, $\operatorname{rank}H_n(X) = \operatorname{rank}Z_n - \operatorname{rank}B_n$.
3. So $\sum(-1)^n c_n = \sum(-1)^n \operatorname{rank}Z_n - \sum(-1)^n \operatorname{rank}B_n$, after re-indexing $n-1 \to n$ in the second sum, which is $\sum(-1)^n \operatorname{rank}H_n(X)$.

Example: $\chi(S^n) = 1 + (-1)^n$ and $\chi(\Sigma_g) = 1 - 2g + 1 = 2 - 2g$.

Watch out: $\chi$ ignores torsion. $\mathbb{RP}^2$ has $\chi = 1 - 1 + 1 = 1$, the same as a point, though its $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$.

cards.title: Compute $H_k(\mathbb{CP}^n)$ for all $k$.
cards.body:
$H_k(\mathbb{CP}^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ for $k = 0,2,4,\dots,2n$ and $0$ otherwise.

$\mathbb{CP}^n$ has one cell in each even dimension $0,2,\dots,2n$ and none in odd dimensions. The cellular chain groups in adjacent degrees are never both nonzero, so every differential is $0$ and $H_k = C_k^{CW}$.

Watch out: this "no room for differentials" argument works because no two cells lie in adjacent dimensions. Compare $\mathbb{RP}^n$, which has a cell in every dimension and torsion.

Tip: the same argument applies to $\mathbb{CP}^\infty = \bigcup_n \mathbb{CP}^n$, which has one cell in each even dimension: $H_k(\mathbb{CP}^\infty) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ for every even $k \ge 0$ and $0$ for odd $k$.

cards.title: Compute $H_*(\Sigma_g)$ for $g \ge 1$ from the cell structure with one 0-cell, $2g$ 1-cells and one 2-cell attached along $\prod_{i=1}^g a_ib_ia_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$.
cards.body:
$H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^{2g}$, $H_2 = \mathbb{Z}$.

1. $d_1 = 0$, because every 1-cell is a loop at the single 0-cell (its end minus its start).
2. By the cellular boundary formula, the 2-cell's boundary has coefficient on $a_i$ equal to the exponent sum of $a_i$ in the word, which is $1 - 1 = 0$; likewise for $b_i$. So $d_2 = 0$.
3. All differentials vanish, so $H_k = C_k$: ranks $1, 2g, 1$.

Check: $\chi(\Sigma_g) = 1 - 2g + 1 = 2 - 2g$, matching the known value.

Watch out: a word of the form $\prod [a_i,b_i]$ always has exponent sum zero in every letter; for a non-orientable surface some letters appear with the same sign twice, which creates torsion.

cards.title: Compute $H_k(T^n)$, where $T^n = (S^1)^n$ has the product cell structure with one cell $e_I$ of dimension $|I|$ for each subset $I \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}$.
cards.body:
$H_k(T^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{\binom{n}{k}}$.

The number of $k$-cells is the number of $k$-element subsets, $\binom nk$. It remains to show every $d_k = 0$.

The cell $e_I$ is a cube $[0,1]^k$ mapping to $T^n$. For each $i \in I$, the two opposite faces $x_i = 0$ and $x_i = 1$ map identically to the same $(k-1)$-cell $e_{I \setminus i}$, with opposite orientations, so their attaching degrees on it are $+1$ and $-1$. The remaining faces map into other $(k-1)$-cells, so they collapse to a point under the quotient onto $e_{I \setminus i}$ and contribute $0$.

Hence $d_k(e_I) = \sum_i \pm(1 - 1)\,e_{I \setminus i} = 0$, and $H_k = C_k = \mathbb{Z}^{\binom nk}$.

Check: $\chi(T^n) = \sum(-1)^k\binom nk = 0$ for $n \ge 1$.

cards.title: Construct a space $M(\mathbb{Z}/m, n)$ for $n \ge 1$, $m \ge 2$, with $H_n \cong \mathbb{Z}/m$ and all other reduced homology groups zero.
cards.body:
$M(\mathbb{Z}/m, n) = S^n \cup_\varphi e^{n+1}$, where $\varphi : S^n \to S^n$ has degree $m$.

A **Moore space** $M(G,n)$ is a CW complex whose only nonzero reduced homology group is $H_n \cong G$.

Cellular chain complex: cells in dimension $0, n, n+1$, with $d_{n+1} = m$ by the cellular boundary formula (the attaching degree of the $(n+1)$-cell on the $n$-cell is $\deg\varphi = m$). So $H_n = \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ and $H_{n+1} = \ker(m) = 0$.

A map of degree $m$ exists: $z \mapsto z^m$ on $S^1$, suspended $n-1$ times.

Example: $n = 1$, $m = 2$ is $\mathbb{RP}^2$.

cards.title: Given an abelian group $G$ and $n \ge 1$, how do you build a CW complex $M(G,n)$ with $H_n \cong G$ and all other reduced homology zero?
cards.body:
Choose $0 \to F_1 \to F_0 \to G \to 0$ with $F_0, F_1$ free abelian; wedge together one $S^n$ for each basis element of $F_0$, then attach an $(n+1)$-cell for each basis element of $F_1$ by a map with the prescribed degrees on the spheres.

Why it works: the cellular chain complex is $0 \to F_1 \to F_0 \to 0$ in degrees $n+1$ and $n$ (plus a 0-cell), with $d_{n+1}$ the inclusion. So $H_n = F_0/F_1 \cong G$ and $H_{n+1} = \ker d_{n+1} = 0$.

Ingredients: a subgroup of a free abelian group is free, so $F_1$ can be taken free. Maps $S^n \to \bigvee_{i=1}^k S^n$ with any prescribed degrees $d_1,\dots,d_k$ exist: collapsing the complement of $k$ disjoint open balls in $S^n$ gives a map $S^n \to \bigvee_k S^n$ of degree $1$ on each sphere (for suitable orientations), and composing with a degree-$d_i$ map on the $i$-th sphere does the rest. For $n=1$ this is a loop given by a word with that abelianization. Only finitely many spheres are involved per cell, since each basis element of $F_1$ has finitely many nonzero coordinates.

Example: $G = \mathbb{Z}^2 \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$ is built as $S^n \vee S^n \vee M(\mathbb{Z}/2,n)$.

cards.title: Define the **lens space** $L(m;l)$ for integers $m \ge 2$ and $l$ coprime to $m$.
cards.body:
$L(m;l) = S^3/(\mathbb{Z}/m)$, where $S^3 \subset \mathbb{C}^2$ and a generator acts by $(z_1,z_2) \mapsto (\zeta z_1, \zeta^l z_2)$ with $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/m}$.

The action is free: if $(\zeta^k z_1, \zeta^{kl}z_2) = (z_1,z_2)$ with $z_1 \ne 0$ then $\zeta^k = 1$; if $z_1 = 0$ then $z_2 \ne 0$ and $\zeta^{kl} = 1$, which gives $m \mid kl$, hence $m \mid k$ since $\gcd(l,m) = 1$.

So $S^3 \to L(m;l)$ is a covering with deck group $\mathbb{Z}/m$, and as $S^3$ is simply connected, $\pi_1(L(m;l)) \cong \mathbb{Z}/m$.

Example: $L(2;1) = \mathbb{RP}^3$.

Watch out: $\pi_1$ and the homology groups do not depend on $l$, so they cannot see it.

cards.title: Let $N_g$ be the connected sum of $g \ge 1$ copies of $\mathbb{RP}^2$, with the cell structure having one 0-cell, $g$ 1-cells $a_1,\dots,a_g$ and one 2-cell attached along $a_1a_1a_2a_2\cdots a_ga_g$. Compute $H_*(N_g)$.
cards.body:
$H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^{g-1} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2 = 0$.

1. $d_1 = 0$ since all 1-cells are loops.
2. Each $a_i$ occurs twice with the same sign, so $d_2(e^2) = 2(a_1 + \cdots + a_g)$, a nonzero element of $\mathbb{Z}^g$. Hence $d_2$ is injective and $H_2 = 0$.
3. $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^g/\mathbb{Z}\cdot 2(1,\dots,1)$. Take the basis $a_1,\dots,a_{g-1}, c = a_1 + \cdots + a_g$ of $\mathbb{Z}^g$. The relation becomes $2c = 0$, so $H_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}^{g-1} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$.

Example: $g = 1$ gives $\mathbb{RP}^2$ with $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$; $g = 2$ is the Klein bottle, with $H_1 = \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}/2$.

Watch out: $H_2 = 0$ for every non-orientable closed surface, while $H_2 = \mathbb{Z}$ for every orientable one.

cards.title: Compute $H_k(S^n \times S^m)$ for $n, m \ge 1$ using the product of the cell structures $e^0 \cup e^n$ on each factor.
cards.body:
$\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $0$ and $n+m$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ in each of the degrees $n$ and $m$ (so $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in degree $n$ when $n = m$); all other $H_k = 0$.

The cells are $e^0$, $e^n \times e^0$, $e^0 \times e^m$ and $e^n \times e^m$. All differentials vanish:

1. $e^n \times e^0$ lies in the subcomplex $S^n \times \mathrm{pt}$, whose cellular chain complex is that of $S^n$ and has all differentials $0$. So $d(e^n \times e^0) = 0$, and likewise $d(e^0 \times e^m) = 0$.
2. $d(e^n \times e^m)$ can only be nonzero on $e^n \times e^0$ (when $m = 1$) or on $e^0 \times e^m$ (when $n = 1$). The coefficient on $e^n \times e^0$ is the degree of the boundary map composed with the projection $p_1 : S^n \times S^m \to S^n$. This is the restriction of $p_1 \circ \Phi$, where $\Phi$ is the characteristic map of the top cell. It extends over the disk $D^{n+1}$, so it is null-homotopic and has degree $0$. The case of $e^0 \times e^m$ is the same with $p_2$.

Check: for $n=m=1$ this is $T^2$ with $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}^2$.

Tip: a second check of step 2. A nonzero coefficient $c$ on $e^n \times e^0$ would give its class order dividing $c$ in $H_n(S^n \times S^m)$. But that class is the image of a generator of $H_n(S^n)$ under the cellular inclusion $S^n \times \mathrm{pt} \hookrightarrow S^n \times S^m$, and $p_1$ maps it back to that generator, which has infinite order.

cards.title: Compute $H_k(\mathbb{RP}^n)$ for all $k$ with the cellular chain complex of the structure with one cell $e^k$ in each dimension $0 \le k \le n$; in particular find the boundary maps $d_k$.
cards.body:
$d_k = 1 + (-1)^k$, so $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_k = \mathbb{Z}/2$ for odd $k < n$, $H_n = \mathbb{Z}$ if $n$ is odd, and all other $H_k = 0$.

1. The cell $e^k$ is attached by the 2-to-1 quotient $S^{k-1} \to \mathbb{RP}^{k-1}$. Composing with $\mathbb{RP}^{k-1} \to \mathbb{RP}^{k-1}/\mathbb{RP}^{k-2} \cong S^{k-1}$ gives a map that is a homeomorphism on each of the two open hemispheres of $S^{k-1}$.
2. The two homeomorphisms differ by the antipodal map of $S^{k-1}$, of degree $(-1)^k$. So the attaching degree is $1 + (-1)^k$, i.e. $d_k = 0$ for odd $k$ and $d_k = 2$ for even $k$.
3. The complex is $\mathbb{Z} \xleftarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \xleftarrow{2} \mathbb{Z} \xleftarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \xleftarrow{2} \cdots$, ending at degree $n$.
4. Odd $k < n$: $\ker d_k = \mathbb{Z}$ and $\operatorname{im}d_{k+1} = 2\mathbb{Z}$, giving $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Even $k>0$: $d_k = 2$ is injective, giving $0$. $k = n$ odd: $d_n = 0$ and nothing hits it, giving $\mathbb{Z}$.

Watch out: for $n$ even, the top $d_n = 2$ is injective, so $H_n = 0$; this reflects that $\mathbb{RP}^{2m}$ is non-orientable.

cards.title: Compute $H_k(L(m;l))$ for all $k$, using the CW structure with one cell in each dimension $0,1,2,3$ in which the 1-skeleton is the circle $C = \{z_2 = 0\}/(\mathbb{Z}/m)$ and the 2-cell is attached to it by a map of degree $m$.
cards.body:
$H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/m$, $H_2 = 0$, $H_3 = \mathbb{Z}$.

Cell structure on $S^3$: the circle $C_0 = \{z_2 = 0\}$ is cut into $m$ arcs by the $m$ points $\zeta^j$; the $m$ discs $D_k = \{z_2 \in e^{2\pi ik/m}\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\}$ have boundary $C_0$ and cut $S^3$ into $m$ 3-balls. The $\mathbb{Z}/m$ action permutes the cells of each dimension simply transitively (using $\gcd(l,m)=1$), so the quotient has one cell in each dimension.

1. $d_1 = 0$: the 1-cell is a loop at the single 0-cell.
2. $d_2 = m$: the boundary of the 2-cell maps onto the circle $C_0/(\mathbb{Z}/m)$ by the $m$-fold quotient map.
3. $d_3 = 0$: the boundary of the 3-cell consists of two discs that both map onto the 2-cell, with opposite orientations, contributing $+1 - 1$.

The complex is $\mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{m} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{0} \mathbb{Z}$, so $H_3 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_2 = \ker m = 0$, $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/m$, $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$.

Check: $H_1 = \pi_1^{ab} = \mathbb{Z}/m$ agrees with $\pi_1(L(m;l)) = \mathbb{Z}/m$.
